title: I2C Bus Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: An RP2040 controller shares the SDA and SCL wires with a VL53L0X distance sensor (0x29) and an SSD1306 OLED display (0x3C). Students step through a write transaction on a bit-level timing diagram, see which device answers with ACK, trigger a NACK with a missing address, and scan the bus.

educational.topic: I2C bus transactions: START, address, ACK, data, STOP
learningObjectives: Trace the parts of an I2C write transaction in order: START, address, R/W, ACK, data, ACK, STOP.
Decode a 7-bit I2C address from hexadecimal to the bits sent on SDA.
Explain how addresses let two devices share the same two wires.
Explain why a missing address produces a NACK and an EIO error.
prerequisites: GPIO pins and config.py pin names
The I2C bus, SDA, SCL, and addresses

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Bit-by-bit step-through of a protocol transaction with a running log
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Students choose the target device, clock speed, and data byte, then Step one bit at a time or Send the whole transaction; Scan bus probes every usable address.
keyQuestions: How does the sensor know a message is meant for it?
Which device drives SDA during the ACK bit?
What happens on the ACK bit when no device has the address?
How long does one write take at 100 kHz and at 400 kHz?
commonMisconceptions: Each I2C device needs its own pair of wires.
The controller sends the ACK bit.
All devices on the bus answer every message.
i2c.scan() checks the wiring, not the addresses.
assessmentOpportunities: Decode 0x29 to binary and check it against the address bits.
Challenge: explain the NACK when sending to 0x50, then confirm the scan result.
Exit ticket: predict the problem when two devices share one address.
